screens.title: What is Identity Federation?
screens.narratorSegment: Identity federation lets people sign in to AWS using credentials managed by a separate identity provider. Concretely, instead of creating IAM users for every employee in each account, you configure AWS to trust assertions from an external IdP. That trust removes duplicate accounts, centralizes policy enforcement like password strength and multi-factor authentication, and enables single sign-on across many AWS accounts and other business applications. For example, when your company uses Azure Active Directory for corporate logins, federation allows those same credentials to gain access to assigned AWS accounts without new passwords. A common misconception is that federation means less security — in fact, it often increases security because corporate controls and MFA remain centrally enforced. Another important point: federated access typically issues temporary credentials, not permanent long-lived keys, which reduces exposure. When you design for federation, think about attribute mapping: how the IdP claims map to AWS groups or IAM roles. A practical question to ask is where group membership is authored: if it stays on-premises, you will either proxy to it or establish a trust so that AWS can evaluate those groups at sign-in. The core takeaway: federation centralizes access control and replaces brittle, duplicated identities with a single managed source of truth.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › What is Identity Federation?
Definition & benefits

Identity federation enables users to authenticate with an external identity provider, enabling centralized controls and SSO across AWS accounts without creating per-user IAM accounts.

  • • Centralizes MFA and password policies under the corporate IdP.
  • • Provides single sign-on to multiple AWS accounts and business apps.
  • • Issues temporary credentials that limit credential exposure.
  • • Reduces administrative overhead and credential sprawl.
Analogy
Think of the IdP as a corporate ID badge. Federation lets that badge open doors (AWS accounts) without issuing new keys for each door.
Key Takeaway

Federation simplifies user lifecycle management and enforces consistent security from a single identity source.

Concrete example
A developer authenticates to Azure AD, clicks the AWS portal tile, and receives a SAML assertion. AWS maps the assertion to an IAM role and issues temporary credentials. The developer can access assigned resources without a separate AWS password.
Common misconception
Federation is not weaker security. When properly configured it enforces corporate MFA and reduces long-lived keys, improving security posture.
Check your understanding
If your org requires Group Policy and trusts with on-prem domains, would federation alone suffice? Consider directory choice for policy support.

screens.title: How SAML 2.0 Federation Works
screens.narratorSegment: SAML 2.0 is the open standard many enterprises use to exchange authentication and authorization information between an identity provider and a service provider. The process starts when a user signs in to the corporate IdP and requests access to an AWS resource or portal. The IdP authenticates the user, builds a SAML assertion — a digitally signed XML document containing the user's identity attributes and group claims — and sends it to AWS. AWS trusts that assertion and maps it to a pre-configured IAM role based on attributes or audience fields. The critical step is attribute mapping: you must align the IdP claims with IAM trust relationships or attribute-based rules so the correct role is assumed. AWS then issues temporary, limited credentials tied to that role; these credentials are time-bound and reduce risk compared to long-lived keys. A frequent mistake is misconfiguring the assertion’s audience or failing to include group claims, which causes login failures or wrong permissions. For example, an employee who belongs to a 'Developers' group should receive a SAML assertion that includes that group so AWS can grant the matching ReadOnly or Dev role. Practically, validate by initiating a login flow and confirming the assumed role and session duration. The core insight: SAML bridges your IdP and AWS using signed assertions that are translated into temporary role-based access.

keyIdea.title: Process summary
keyIdea.text: SAML assertions carry identity and group claims; AWS maps these to IAM roles to grant temporary credentials.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › SAML 2.0 Flow
Step-by-step flow
1. Authenticate
User signs in to IdP and proves identity.
2. Generate assertion
IdP issues a signed XML assertion with claims.
3. Send to AWS
Assertion is POSTed to AWS or Identity Center as trusted input.
4. Assume role
AWS maps claims to an IAM role and issues temporary credentials.
Attribute mapping
Ensure group or role attributes in the assertion match IAM role trust policies or Identity Center mappings.
Common mistake
Missing audience, wrong name ID format, or absent group claims will prevent correct role assumption.
Concrete example
An IdP returns an assertion with claim 'groups': ['Developers']. AWS maps the 'Developers' claim to the Dev IAM role and issues temporary credentials for one hour. The user can list resources allowed by that role.
Validation steps
  1. Confirm the IdP audience and issuer match the AWS trust configuration.
  2. Ensure required attributes and group claims are present in the SAML assertion.
  3. Log in and inspect the assumed role and session duration to verify permissions.
Key Takeaway

SAML assertions translate corporate identities into temporary AWS role access; attribute mapping is the bridge.

screens.title: AWS Directory Service Options
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Directory Service provides three common approaches to integrate directory needs in the cloud. First, AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a fully managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS. It supports Group Policy, trusts, and can be joined to your on-premises AD through a trust relationship. Use it if you require native Windows features or cross-domain trusts. Second, AD Connector acts as a lightweight proxy between AWS services and your on-premises Microsoft AD without copying accounts to the cloud. It forwards authentication requests to the on-prem directory, which keeps all credentials and group memberships on-premises. This is ideal when you want to avoid directory replication but still let cloud resources authenticate with corporate identities. Third, Simple AD is a low-cost managed directory powered by Samba 4; it is suitable for basic directory needs, particularly for Linux-based applications that do not require trust relationships or Group Policy. A common decision pitfall is choosing Simple AD when you actually need Group Policy or trusts; evaluate feature needs carefully. Consider operational factors like replication, high availability, and backup. The right choice balances functionality, cost, and your requirement to keep identity authoritative on-premises versus in-cloud.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Directory Service Options
Architectural choices
AWS Managed Microsoft AD
Fully managed AD compatible with on-prem AD. Supports trusts, Group Policy, and Windows workload integration.
AD Connector
A proxy that forwards authentication to your on-premises AD. No cloud replication; keeps credentials on-premises.
Simple AD
Low-cost, Samba-based directory for basic needs. Does not support trusts with on-premises AD.
Decision guide
  • • Need Group Policy or trusts? Choose Managed Microsoft AD.
  • • Want no replication and to keep credentials on-premises? Use AD Connector.
  • • Low-cost directory for Linux apps without trusts? Simple AD fits.
Concrete scenario
An enterprise requiring Group Policy for Windows servers and trusts between domains should deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and set up a trust to on-premises AD. If policy enforcement stays on-premises and replication is not desired, AD Connector forwards authentication to the existing AD without copying users to the cloud.
Operational note
Consider maintenance: managed AD provides high availability and backups; AD Connector reduces data duplication but depends on network connectivity to on-premises AD.
Key Takeaway

Pick the directory option that matches feature needs: trusts and Group Policy, proxy-only, or lightweight Samba-powered directory.

screens.title: AWS Managed Microsoft AD — Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides a full-featured, highly available Microsoft Active Directory hosted in AWS. Use this option when your workloads require native Windows features such as Group Policy, Kerberos authentication, or trust relationships with other domains. Managed Microsoft AD runs domain controllers managed by AWS, removes the operational burden of patching and replication, and supports establishing trusts to your on-premises AD so users can authenticate against their existing accounts. A practical example: if you run Windows Server instances joined to AD and need Group Policy to deploy security settings, a managed AD in AWS is the proper choice. One misconception is that managed AD requires you to abandon on-premises AD; it does not — you can establish trusts and let on-premises users access AWS resources through the managed directory. Operationally, consider network connectivity, domain controllers placement in multiple subnets for resilience, and cost compared to AD Connector. Also confirm application compatibility: some legacy services expect an actual Microsoft AD and its features. The key idea: choose Managed Microsoft AD when you need full Windows directory functionality in the cloud with managed operational overhead reduction.

keyIdea.title: When to choose it
keyIdea.text: Pick AWS Managed Microsoft AD when you require native Windows AD features, Group Policy, or trust relationships with on-premises domains.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Managed Microsoft AD
Feature summary
  • • Fully managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS with high availability.
  • • Supports Group Policy for Windows workloads and domain joins.
  • • Allows trust relationships with on-premises AD for seamless authentication.
  • • AWS manages domain controllers and replication.
Concrete scenario
A company running Windows-based applications needs Group Policy templates and trusts to the corporate AD. Deploying Managed Microsoft AD lets those servers join the domain and receive policies without hosting domain controllers in EC2.
Misconception check
Managed AD does not force you to copy users to the cloud; it supports trusts that allow on-premises users to authenticate.
Operational considerations
Plan subnets for domain controllers across Availability Zones for resilience, configure secure network connectivity for trust links, and review cost versus AD Connector if you do not need Group Policy.
Key Takeaway

Managed AD is the right fit when full Windows directory features and trusts are required and you prefer AWS to manage availability and replication.

screens.title: AD Connector — Proxy to On-Prem AD
screens.narratorSegment: AD Connector is a directory gateway that forwards authentication requests from AWS services directly to your on-premises Active Directory. It does not synchronize or replicate user accounts into the cloud. Use AD Connector when you want users to authenticate with their corporate accounts and you want to avoid maintaining a separate cloud directory. Practically, AD Connector is ideal for organizations that have strict controls keeping credentials on-premises or that want to avoid user lifecycle duplication. A typical use case: allowing EC2 instances or applications in AWS to authenticate using your existing AD accounts while the authoritative directory remains on-premises. Important caveats include network dependency — AD Connector requires reliable connectivity between AWS and the on-prem AD — and potential latency for authentication calls. A common mistake is selecting AD Connector when Group Policy or trusts are required in-cloud; AD Connector cannot act as a full domain controller. You should also design for availability and secure connectivity, for example by using multiple connectors across subnets and ensuring firewall rules allow necessary traffic. The essential benefit is that AD Connector preserves a single source of truth without data replication in AWS.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › AD Connector
How it works
AD Connector forwards authentication requests to your on-premises AD, acting as a gateway. No user data is copied to AWS; the on-premises directory remains authoritative.
When to choose it
  • • You must keep credentials on-premises for compliance.
  • • You want to avoid directory replication and synchronization.
  • • You have reliable network connectivity and low latency requirements.
Pitfall
Do not use AD Connector if you need Group Policy or in-cloud domain controllers. It cannot serve as a managed AD for Windows domain features.
Operational checklist
  1. Deploy connectors in multiple subnets for availability.
  2. Ensure necessary ports and firewall rules to reach on-prem AD.
  3. Monitor latency and authentication failures as part of operations.
Key Takeaway

AD Connector is the right choice when you must keep credential authority on-premises while still enabling AWS services to authenticate users.

screens.title: Simple AD — Lightweight Directory
screens.narratorSegment: Simple AD is a low-cost, managed directory option built on Samba 4 that offers basic Active Directory-compatible features. It is appropriate when you have straightforward user authentication needs, especially for Linux-based workloads or development environments that do not require Group Policy or trust relationships with on-premises domains. Simple AD is intentionally lightweight; it reduces cost and operational complexity but does not support advanced AD features like trusts or native Windows Group Policy objects. A common mistake is to select Simple AD for an environment that later needs trusts with corporate domains — in that case you should migrate to AWS Managed Microsoft AD. Use Simple AD for small teams, internal tools, or when you need directory-compatible authentication without the full footprint of a Microsoft AD. Also consider how user lifecycle management will be handled: Simple AD holds its own user directory, so decide whether you want separate application-focused accounts or to federate to corporate identities instead. The practical benefit is simplicity and lower cost, at the expense of advanced Windows integration. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Simple AD
Overview
Simple AD offers a Samba-based Active Directory-compatible directory for basic authentication and directory services at a lower cost. It is not a drop-in replacement for Microsoft AD when Group Policy or trusts are needed.
Use cases
  • • Lightweight authentication for Linux workloads or internal tools.
  • • Small teams that don’t need advanced AD features.
  • • Cost-sensitive environments where full Microsoft AD is unnecessary.
Migration note
If your environment later requires Group Policy or trusts, plan to migrate to AWS Managed Microsoft AD because Simple AD lacks those capabilities.
Practical example
A small development team uses Simple AD for internal authentication across a set of Linux servers and developer tools. It provides directory-compatible logins without the cost or operational footprint of a managed Microsoft AD.
Key Takeaway

Simple AD is cost-effective for basic directory needs, but not suitable when Windows AD features or trusts are required.

screens.title: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO)
screens.narratorSegment: AWS IAM Identity Center is the recommended service for centralized single sign-on across multiple AWS accounts. It provides a user portal where employees can click into assigned accounts and applications. You can manage identities directly in Identity Center, or connect it to an external source such as AWS Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector, or any SAML 2.0 compatible IdP. The key operational concept is the permission set: a collection of permissions that Identity Center provisions as an IAM role in target accounts. When you assign a user or group a permission set for a specific account, Identity Center creates the corresponding role and grants the user temporary access through the console. This pattern decouples permission management from individual AWS accounts and enforces consistent roles across accounts. A common misconception is that Identity Center automatically maps every group claim; you must configure group mappings and permission sets deliberately. How Identity Center works

screens.title: Hands-on: Enable IAM Identity Center & Test SSO
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through enabling Identity Center and validating a simple SSO flow. First, enable IAM Identity Center in the console. This sets up a default directory or connects to your organization. Next, create a user named dev-user and optionally a Developers group, then add the user to that group. The crucial step is the permission set: create ReadOnlyAccess as a permission set and name it ReadOnlyAccess-Dev. Assign the Developers group to a member AWS account with that permission set. Provisioning will create the corresponding IAM role in the target account, so allow a few minutes for completion. Now test the SSO experience by accepting the invitation email as the new user, setting a password, and signing in to the user portal. From the portal, select the assigned AWS account and the Management Console link associated with the ReadOnly permission set. Confirm that you can list resources like S3 buckets but cannot perform write actions. A common validation step is to intentionally attempt a forbidden action, such as creating an S3 bucket, to confirm the permission set is enforced. This exercise demonstrates centralized provisioning, role creation in member accounts, and the end-user experience. After testing, reflect on where Identity Center removed manual account management in your environment and what additional groups or permission sets you would need in production.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step
  1. Enable IAM Identity Center in the AWS console and allow setup to finish.
  2. Create user dev-user and record the user portal URL from the invitation.
  3. Create Developers group and add dev-user to the group.

  • • Log in and list S3 buckets to verify read access.
  • • Attempt a denied action like creating a bucket to confirm restrictions.
Misconfiguration warning
If provisioning stalls, check that your organization and account settings allow Identity Center to create roles in the target accounts, and that you have sufficient permissions in the management account.

This activity demonstrates how Identity Center centralizes account access and creates consistent IAM roles across accounts with a single assignment action.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Identity & Directories
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the critical concepts you should remember. Identity federation allows users to authenticate to AWS with external credentials, enabling SSO and centralized policy enforcement. AWS Directory Service provides three main options: AWS Managed Microsoft AD for full Windows features and trusts, AD Connector to proxy to on-premises AD without replication, and Simple AD for lightweight Samba-based directory needs. AWS IAM Identity Center centralizes multi-account access using permission sets that provision IAM roles in member accounts, simplifying governance and auditing. SAML 2.0 is the common standard for enterprise federation: the IdP issues a signed assertion mapping attributes and group claims to IAM roles for temporary access. screens.title: What to Remember

fullNarratorScript:
As your cloud environment grows, managing separate IAM users across accounts becomes untenable. In this lesson you will learn the principle of identity federation: letting users sign in to AWS with credentials managed by an external identity provider. That single sign-on experience reduces credential sprawl, centralizes multi-factor authentication and password policy enforcement, and aligns cloud access with corporate identity controls. You will see how AWS Directory Service offers several deployment patterns — a managed Microsoft Active Directory for full Windows functionality, AD Connector as a gateway to on-premises directories, and Simple AD for lightweight directory needs. We will also walk through AWS IAM Identity Center to deliver multi-account SSO and permission sets, the SAML 2.0 mechanism that exchanges signed assertions for temporary AWS access, and Amazon Cognito for application-level user pools and identity pools. By the end of this module you will know which service to pick when you need Group Policy, when to proxy to on-premises AD, and when to use Cognito for mobile apps. Think about one example in your environment: where would federation reduce risk and operational work? That will guide your design choices.

These learning objectives are practical skills you should walk away with. First, you will be able to explain identity federation: why delegating authentication to an external identity provider reduces credential sprawl and makes multi-factor enforcement consistent. Second, you will differentiate the AWS Directory Service options so you can pick managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector, or Simple AD based on needs such as Group Policy support, trust relationships, and cost. Third, you will understand how SAML 2.0 operates as the technical glue for enterprise federation, taking a digitally signed assertion and exchanging it for temporary AWS role credentials. Fourth, you will be able to implement AWS IAM Identity Center to centralize SSO across multiple AWS accounts and define permission sets that translate to IAM roles. Each objective ties directly to real-world tasks: describing the flow, choosing a directory pattern, configuring Identity Center, and validating that a federated user can access an assigned account. As you study the next screens, map each practical step back to these objectives to ensure you can perform and justify the design choices.

This second objectives slide focuses on application and validation skills you should practice. First, you will be able to map a corporate on-premises Active Directory to an AWS directory option and justify that choice in terms of Group Policy, trust requirements, and cost. Second, you will configure a simple SAML 2.0 integration: register AWS as a service provider, map attributes and group claims, and confirm that the assertion maps to an IAM role for temporary access. Third, you will create a Cognito user pool and enable a social identity provider so application users can sign in with Google or Facebook, and then exchange that identity for temporary AWS credentials using an identity pool. Fourth, you will validate the authentication experience: log in to the IAM Identity Center user portal, click into an assigned account, and confirm read-only or restricted access based on the permission set. These objectives are hands-on: completing them shows you can both design and operate federation and directory integrations.

Identity federation lets people sign in to AWS using credentials managed by a separate identity provider. Concretely, instead of creating IAM users for every employee in each account, you configure AWS to trust assertions from an external IdP. That trust removes duplicate accounts, centralizes policy enforcement like password strength and multi-factor authentication, and enables single sign-on across many AWS accounts and other business applications. For example, when your company uses Azure Active Directory for corporate logins, federation allows those same credentials to gain access to assigned AWS accounts without new passwords. A common misconception is that federation means less security — in fact, it often increases security because corporate controls and MFA remain centrally enforced. Another important point: federated access typically issues temporary credentials, not permanent long-lived keys, which reduces exposure. When you design for federation, think about attribute mapping: how the IdP claims map to AWS groups or IAM roles. A practical question to ask is where group membership is authored: if it stays on-premises, you will either proxy to it or establish a trust so that AWS can evaluate those groups at sign-in. The core takeaway: federation centralizes access control and replaces brittle, duplicated identities with a single managed source of truth.

SAML 2.0 is the open standard many enterprises use to exchange authentication and authorization information between an identity provider and a service provider. The process starts when a user signs in to the corporate IdP and requests access to an AWS resource or portal. The IdP authenticates the user, builds a SAML assertion — a digitally signed XML document containing the user's identity attributes and group claims — and sends it to AWS. AWS trusts that assertion and maps it to a pre-configured IAM role based on attributes or audience fields. The critical step is attribute mapping: you must align the IdP claims with IAM trust relationships or attribute-based rules so the correct role is assumed. AWS then issues temporary, limited credentials tied to that role; these credentials are time-bound and reduce risk compared to long-lived keys. A frequent mistake is misconfiguring the assertion’s audience or failing to include group claims, which causes login failures or wrong permissions. For example, an employee who belongs to a 'Developers' group should receive a SAML assertion that includes that group so AWS can grant the matching ReadOnly or Dev role. Practically, validate by initiating a login flow and confirming the assumed role and session duration. The core insight: SAML bridges your IdP and AWS using signed assertions that are translated into temporary role-based access.

AWS Directory Service provides three common approaches to integrate directory needs in the cloud. First, AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a fully managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS. It supports Group Policy, trusts, and can be joined to your on-premises AD through a trust relationship. Use it if you require native Windows features or cross-domain trusts. Second, AD Connector acts as a lightweight proxy between AWS services and your on-premises Microsoft AD without copying accounts to the cloud. It forwards authentication requests to the on-prem directory, which keeps all credentials and group memberships on-premises. This is ideal when you want to avoid directory replication but still let cloud resources authenticate with corporate identities. Third, Simple AD is a low-cost managed directory powered by Samba 4; it is suitable for basic directory needs, particularly for Linux-based applications that do not require trust relationships or Group Policy. A common decision pitfall is choosing Simple AD when you actually need Group Policy or trusts; evaluate feature needs carefully. Consider operational factors like replication, high availability, and backup. The right choice balances functionality, cost, and your requirement to keep identity authoritative on-premises versus in-cloud.

AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides a full-featured, highly available Microsoft Active Directory hosted in AWS. Use this option when your workloads require native Windows features such as Group Policy, Kerberos authentication, or trust relationships with other domains. Managed Microsoft AD runs domain controllers managed by AWS, removes the operational burden of patching and replication, and supports establishing trusts to your on-premises AD so users can authenticate against their existing accounts. A practical example: if you run Windows Server instances joined to AD and need Group Policy to deploy security settings, a managed AD in AWS is the proper choice. One misconception is that managed AD requires you to abandon on-premises AD; it does not — you can establish trusts and let on-premises users access AWS resources through the managed directory. Operationally, consider network connectivity, domain controllers placement in multiple subnets for resilience, and cost compared to AD Connector. Also confirm application compatibility: some legacy services expect an actual Microsoft AD and its features. The key idea: choose Managed Microsoft AD when you need full Windows directory functionality in the cloud with managed operational overhead reduction.

AD Connector is a directory gateway that forwards authentication requests from AWS services directly to your on-premises Active Directory. It does not synchronize or replicate user accounts into the cloud. Use AD Connector when you want users to authenticate with their corporate accounts and you want to avoid maintaining a separate cloud directory. Practically, AD Connector is ideal for organizations that have strict controls keeping credentials on-premises or that want to avoid user lifecycle duplication. A typical use case: allowing EC2 instances or applications in AWS to authenticate using your existing AD accounts while the authoritative directory remains on-premises. Important caveats include network dependency — AD Connector requires reliable connectivity between AWS and the on-prem AD — and potential latency for authentication calls. A common mistake is selecting AD Connector when Group Policy or trusts are required in-cloud; AD Connector cannot act as a full domain controller. You should also design for availability and secure connectivity, for example by using multiple connectors across subnets and ensuring firewall rules allow necessary traffic. The essential benefit is that AD Connector preserves a single source of truth without data replication in AWS.

Simple AD is a low-cost, managed directory option built on Samba 4 that offers basic Active Directory-compatible features. It is appropriate when you have straightforward user authentication needs, especially for Linux-based workloads or development environments that do not require Group Policy or trust relationships with on-premises domains. Simple AD is intentionally lightweight; it reduces cost and operational complexity but does not support advanced AD features like trusts or native Windows Group Policy objects. A common mistake is to select Simple AD for an environment that later needs trusts with corporate domains — in that case you should migrate to AWS Managed Microsoft AD. Use Simple AD for small teams, internal tools, or when you need directory-compatible authentication without the full footprint of a Microsoft AD. Also consider how user lifecycle management will be handled: Simple AD holds its own user directory, so decide whether you want separate application-focused accounts or to federate to corporate identities instead. The practical benefit is simplicity and lower cost, at the expense of advanced Windows integration. Simple AD — Lightweight Directory means choose simple ad for low-cost, basic directory needs when advanced windows features and trusts are not required.. In practical terms, low-cost directory for basic needs and linux-based applications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
